note.note:
History:
• 26-year-old female with known asthma reports 2–3 days of new chest tightness, wheeze, dry cough, and shortness of breath that began while running and now occurs with brisk walking.  
• Uses salbutamol (blue inhaler) when symptomatic with little relief; preventer (“brown” Clenil/beclomethasone) taken 3 puffs twice daily.  
• No sputum, fever, chest pain, or prior hospital admissions. Last asthma attack 3–4 years ago. No recent peak-flow measurement (baseline ≈380 L/min).  
• Triggers/associations: exercise; uncertain environmental factor.  
• No oral steroid or antibiotic courses in the past; last asthma review ~2 years ago.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma (well-controlled until current episode).  
• Hay fever.  
• Possible eczema (topical treatments in use).  
• Family: brother with asthma, sister with eczema.  
• Allergies: denies drug allergies; seasonal allergic rhinitis (hay fever).  
Medications:  
– Salbutamol inhaler, dose/route/frequency not documented (PRN).  
– Clenil (beclomethasone) inhaler 3 puffs BID (inhaled).  
– Cetraben cream, dose/route/frequency not documented (topical).  
– Hydrocortisone cream, dose/route/frequency not documented (topical).  
Social history, smoking/alcohol: not recorded.

Physical Examination:
• Tele-consultation; no in-person exam performed.  
• Patient appears able to converse in full sentences (inferred).  
• No sputum production reported.  
• Vitals, lung auscultation, peak-flow: Not recorded.

Impression:
Likely mild asthma exacerbation (exercise/possible allergen-triggered) with sub-optimal controller dosing.  
DDx consistent with transcript:
1. Asthma exacerbation – fits history of asthma, new wheeze, ↑ reliever use, poor response.  
2. Viral URTI–triggered asthma – possible given acute onset, cough but no systemic symptoms.

Management Plan:
• Increase preventer (Clenil) to 4 puffs twice daily while awaiting review.  
• Salbutamol inhaler up to every 2 hours PRN; if this frequency required or symptoms worsen, proceed to Emergency Department.  
• Arrange face-to-face GP appointment within a few days for chest exam and peak-flow; consider oral steroids and/or antibiotics based on findings.  
• Educate on recognizing red-flag symptoms (inability to speak, use of reliever > every 2 hours, nighttime worsening).  
• Review inhaler technique during upcoming appointment.  
• No new oral medications prescribed during tele-visit.

Patient Summary:
Young asthmatic woman developed exercise-related SOB and wheeze over 3 days, minimally relieved by salbutamol. Advised to up-titrate inhaled steroids, use reliever as needed, and obtain prompt in-person review; seek emergency care if deterioration.

Key Takeaways:
• Increase brown inhaler to 4 puffs twice daily.  
• Use blue inhaler when needed, but if required more often than every 2 hours, go to A&E.  
• Book and attend face-to-face GP visit within the next few days for full assessment.

Next Steps:
• Objective peak-flow and lung auscultation at GP visit.  
• Consider oral corticosteroids/antibiotics if evidence of significant exacerbation or infection.  
• Re-establish regular asthma reviews (annual) once acute episode resolved.
